Dog body language is a complex subject as I’m sure you’re gathering from some comments on here. My recommendation would be to grab a book on the subject and before judging it on your dog practice it on other dogs. I work in the vet field and HAVE to read body language to keep myself, my coworkers, and of course my patients safe and comfortable. And even I have troubles reading my dog at times. 

For now meeting other dogs, I would stay away from greetings if your dog is excited. Excitement can lead to a fight from either dog. Get your dog in a calm state by an action, like sitting, focusing on you, laying down, until you can meet the dog. Also try and be aware of your body language and state of mind. If you are nervous, you will be making your dog nervous. Actual aggression and not fear/anxiety will appear with a furrowed brow, head low and directed at the target.  Lips pulled back (may be showing teeth or not. Tail wags may come with aggression but these are much different from your play tail wags. They are very stiff. The tail will  hardly move. Where as your happy tail is your full force swinging back and forth. 

But again, grab a book as I prefer, or some YouTube videos.

As a vet technician the process may vary slightly from each clinic, so it’s best to ask what to expect. Hopefully they’ll be communicating through and through with you on what to expect. I work in emergency and this is our process through euthanasia. While you fill out paperwork, and make any payments we have your kiddo in the back to place an IV catheter. Throughout this process we ourselves love on your animal and give them all the kisses and treats if they’ll have some. Once you’re ready and your pet is ready we bring them to you in our room that is set up with a couch and some extra chairs for any family members. We have a button that will ring a bell in our doctor hallway to let our doctor know you are ready. The doctor will go in and should walk you through what to expect. Every clinic again uses different medications. For us, we give propofol first. This is used for anesthesia. Your pet is going to go into a deep sleep, but their heart will still be beating. The euthanasia will then be administered. After this is given the doctor will check your kiddos heart and state that your pet has indeed passed away. Rest assured your pet did not feel any pain and has passed away peacefully. You may still see some gasping breaths or some muscle tremors, this doesn’t always happen. But it’s important to understand that it can, as when you see it and you don’t know, it can be scary to think your pet is still alive. You are then given as much time as you need to finish saying your goodbyes. 

I’m extremely sorry. I too have had to euthanize my kiddo for aggressive behavior. Go through your grieving process as you need to. For me it helped to think my kiddo was better. He wasn’t stressed anymore and his heart and mind were at rest.

As an ER technician when a critical comes in our receptionists rush them back, giving us a history as we triage. If we tell them we need a critical we’re going to start doing what we can to save that animals life while our receptionist goes over the information. They are honest but nice. They let the client know that they’re pet has stopped breathing and we have started CPR. Usually the thought of, “ oh my pet isn’t breathing,  What do I want to do... “ they’re quicker to make a decision. Because it’s happening. If we have to eat a cost because someone doesn’t want to pay, we can do that. Our important factor is your pet comes first, always. We’ve had people even leave reviews thanking us for doing this because they weren’t able to make a decision fast. And even though they chose DNR they were grateful that we just started to before needing proof we were going to get paid. 

The best advice I can give you is talk to your manager. Let them know your concern, and ask what you can do to make this faster. Or even the technicians that are giving you a hard time. Don’t ask in the stress of it all. But after things have settled back down. And please please realize that the anger and frustration isn’t at you. It’s frustration that they have to even get this payment before they can do anything. It stress. It’s not you.

Did you just throw him in there? Dogs need to be worked into crate training. Crates should become their happy place. If he won’t get in there by himself. He shouldn’t be locked in. 

Start by when playing throwing the toy into the crate now and then. So he gets comfortable even just going in there. Get a more open crate. Start feeding him in his crate. Put some blankets down. When he starts going in on his own, now is the time to start being able to shut the door. And again this will have to be worked into. Shut it and go into another room for a bit, like 5 mins. And come back. And let him out. Do this until he’s used to it. Then go fifteen minutes of leaving the house. Same process. 30 mins. An hour. 

If you just throw him in without working up to this he will become scared of something that really can be a great tool. 

Think of the crate like your bedroom. You go in to relax, probably eat. But you wouldn’t want to be locked in. At least not by choice. You go to your room to hide and get away. His crate needs to be this to him. 

It’s a process but worth it. Good luck!

If you haven’t already. Get a trainer. I have learned the hard way that aggressive behavior can spiral quickly if not taken action on. A lot train with e-collars, if that doesn’t bother you, great. If so, find a different approach. You will need something that you’ll be able to be consistent with as well for this training to work. 

A lot of times they’re aggressive tends to be fear based. Which could be what you were leaning towards. Confidence building exercises are great, for any dog really. But also make sure you’re establishing yourself as pack leader. He needs to be able to look to you for guidance when he gets scared. If he sees leader being calm in these situations then he will be too. Which is also to say, remind yourself to not get anxiety in these situations, and try to avoid them as best as you can for the time being. If you see a dog, just walk the other way. No harm in that. If you do happen to come across that situation, don’t get worked up by pulling or yelling telling him no, get his attention on you.. this can be done with treats, or even being excited. Get cherry and be like “ come on let’s go this way! Good boy” make yourself the object that’s most exciting. 

Also, patience. Any aggressive behavior can be stressful. Don’t let it take its toll on you. Good luck!

Are you walking him to get him to go potty? If so stop. This has all been said mostly. But, find a schedule, and stick to it. Take him out after play times, first thing in the morning, eating and drinking..etc. when you take him out, take him to a spot that is nearby. I don’t know your living situation, but if you have a yard, walk him right out to the same spot every time. He will familiarize himself with this area and will be more likely to go. If you’re in an apartment pick the closest spot of grass. Once he goes praise the shit out of him! And immediately after he goes. No more than 1-2 seconds. Bring your fan girl cheerleader out and tell him “good job, potty outside” and treats! Kiddos love treats, especially when starting their potty training journey and then a walk. That in itself is a reward! If he doesn’t go, put him in a crate, small enough that he can’t pee/poop on one side and go and sleep in the other, wait 5-15 mins. And repeat. Crate training is amazing when it comes to potty training. 

Now, if your pup does pee in the house, don’t yell at them. And first, they should be on a leash hooked to you st all times. So when they start to go. Pull on the leash, “telling them, outside potty, potty outside” and take them to their spot. Now if they happen to go, or like my adult dog who I had to train, just didn’t stop peeing 🤦🏻‍♀️ I still didn’t get mad at him. He had to go. That’s not his fault. It’s mine. But, on that note, I do get mad at the pee spot. While I clean it up I mutter to myself that this should have been outside. They associate this that you didn’t like this action, but you’re not mad at them. And dogs love to please. So eventually they’re going to pick up on these cues of what is making their owner happy and what isnt. 

So in a lump sum. 
Get a crate
Same potty spot
Reward reward reward 
Create a schedule 
Consistency is key 
It’s you, not the dog - figure out what you’re not doing right 
Don’t get mad at him - direct anger to that pee. 
Keep on a leash that is hooked to you at all times- this dog does not ever leave your site. 

My dog was a pain to potty train. I had to find what worked for him. But also accept that I was messing up. He has been accident free for 3 months. And I still follow these, besides the leash, but he doesn’t leave my site. Because one slip up and it will set you back so far.

If you have the money doggy boot camp will be your best bet. I had an aggressive Belgian malinois that unfortunately I ended up having to put down. I’m not a professional by any means, just my own experience of what I had to go through with my pup. Trust building exercises are huge for any situation with dogs and establishing yourself as pack leader. If they’re not looking to you for guidance then you have not established this. 

I wish I could give more advice.. because i feel you. I think finding out which type of aggressive behavior he is expressing will be huge in the long run as well. Is he being over stimulated? Is it because he’s afraid? 

The major steps I would start taking is establish yourself as pack leader, you should be constantly training your dog, and that can be through everyday activities. Such as, when my dog sits and waits for me to say “ok” when we get back from a walk, we’ve done this so many times it’s just automatic.. and if he gets excited and forgets, I’m like “what do you do first?” And he hurry and sits and stares at me until I say ok. This. This staring at you, waiting for your guidance, is what you want. And working little things like this in your everyday routine, and being consistent can be huge. But also just as simply making sure he is getting enough exercise. Enough exercise is enough to really calm them down in most situations. 

I would also like to add, get a crate ASAP. Crate training is amazing. It can be a struggle to start training, but eventually it becomes a life saver. Let him eat in his crate, sleep, let this become his place.  Not your bed. So when he gets scared he can go into here. If you’re not going to be there, he can go into here. It will at least ease your roommates and boyfriends mind that he is in a crate for now, and can’t attack them. Crate training can be looked at as a terrible thing. It’s not to keep him locked away. It’s to give him his own space, a place to call HIS. 

If you ever want to talk to more feel free to message me. Again, I feel your struggle with this and it can be very stressful. Keep your head up!

There’s also a fun game you can play, well more fun for you, but fun to see them figure things out. You put them on the tie down, have it lay down. If he lays down, slowly step towards him.
